### `legacy_audit.report.deck_builder`

File: `legacy_audit/report/deck_builder.py`

Build ``deck.json``: the management presentation as data, rendered as HTML and as PPTX.

Slides follow ``docs/plan.md`` § Outputs (executive summary, functional view, current
architecture, technical deep-dive, target architecture, plan, risks and next steps). Numbers come
from the run's facts (``audit-summary.json``, ``effort.json``, entity files); interpretation comes
from the validated enrichment. A slide part whose enrichment stage is missing shows a placeholder
naming the prompt to run, so the deck can be built straight after a scan.

Block types: ``kpis``, ``bullets``, ``text``, ``chart`` (bar, doughnut, line; one series),
``table``, ``diagram`` (Mermaid source, plus a PNG path once rendered) and ``placeholder``.

- internal helpers: `_num`, `_cut`, `_get`

### `legacy_audit.report.diagrams`

File: `legacy_audit/report/diagrams.py`

Mermaid diagrams generated from the facts (code edges, integrations, batch jobs).

Every node and arrow comes from a fact; labels are escaped for Mermaid. Large estates are capped
(``MAX_NODES``) with a note, since a diagram past that size is unreadable; the catalogues hold
the full lists.

- **class `Diagram`** `@dataclass`

- `integration_map(rd: RunData) -> Diagram`: Components and the external systems they reach (databases, queues, hosts, files).
- `batch_chains(rd: RunData) -> list[Diagram]`: One flowchart per scheduler: jobs inside their boxes, dependencies with their condition, and what each job runs (scripts, programs, Spring Batch jobs, steps).
- `layered(architecture: dict[str, Any]) -> Diagram | None`: The agent's layers (enrichment ``architecture.layers``) as coloured bands, top down.
- `current_to_target(rd: RunData, target: dict[str, Any]) -> Diagram | None`: Legacy components (scan) on the left, target components (enrichment) on the right, an arrow for each 'replaces'.

- internal helpers: `_label`, `_run_targets`

### `legacy_audit.report.flows`

File: `legacy_audit/report/flows.py`

Screen flows and batch flows built from the scan facts alone.

A **screen flow** follows one screen: where the user comes from, the services it calls (the ones
that load it and the ones its forms and links submit to), the tables those services read and
write (create, read, update, delete, from the SQL each service reaches), the external systems
they call, and the screens the user goes to next.

A **batch flow** follows one batch: an Autosys box with its jobs, or a job that runs on its own
(Autosys, cron, JCL, Spring Batch). It shows what starts it (schedule, condition, watched file),
its steps in order and what each runs, the tables and files it reads and writes, what runs
before and after it, and the failure handling found in the scheduler definition.

Both are deterministic: every node and arrow is a fact, with evidence. The functional report
adds the Copilot agent's plain-language description on top (``enrichment/functional.json``);
the technical report shows them as they are. ``columns`` and ``edges`` feed the PPTX, which
draws the same flow with native shapes; ``mermaid`` feeds the HTML pages.

- **class `Node`** `@dataclass`
  - fields: `key`, `label`, `kind`, `detail`
- **class `Flow`** `@dataclass`
  - fields: `id`, `kind`, `name`, `slug`, `component`, `summary`, `columns`, `edges`, `tables`, `systems`, `services`, `steps`, `before`, `after`, `schedule`, `on_failure`, `evidence`, `note`, `files`
  - `mermaid() -> str`
  - `deck_block() -> dict[str, Any]`: The flow as a deck block: columns of nodes and the arrows between them.
- `to_mermaid(columns: list[tuple[str, list[Node]]], edges: list[tuple[str, str, str]]) -> str`
- `crud_words(letters: str) -> str`
- `screen_flows(rd: RunData) -> list[Flow]`
- `parse_schedule(schedule: str | None, scheduler: str) -> dict[str, Any]`: Days of the week (0 = Monday), start times and a plain sentence, from a cron line or the Autosys schedule attributes. Unknown shapes keep the raw text.
- `batch_flows(rd: RunData) -> list[Flow]`
- `crud_matrix(rd: RunData, group_by: str='component') -> dict[str, Any]`: Rows (components, or capabilities via ``group_by``) x tables, cells = CRUD letters, from the SQL each statement's component runs. Returned sorted by the busiest tables.
- `tables_used_together(rd: RunData, limit: int=40) -> list[tuple[str, str, int]]`: Pairs of tables used in the same SQL statement (joins, sub-queries), with how many statements; a proxy for relationships when the DDL's keys are not parsed.
- `data_map_mermaid(rd: RunData) -> str`: Tables as nodes, coloured, joined when they appear in the same statement.
- `week_grid(flows: list[Flow]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]`: One row per scheduled batch: its start times on each day of the week.
- `code_comments(rd: RunData, f: Flow, limit: int=6) -> list[dict[str, Any]]`: The header comment of each source file a batch runs (``{file, lines}``), read from the scanned source when it is on this machine; what the programs say about themselves.
- internal class `_Index`: Lookups shared by both kinds of flow. Methods: `__init__`, `owners`, `tables_of`, `systems_of`, `table_rows`
- internal helpers: `_crud`, `_service_label`, `_screen_label`, `_system_label`, `_cap`, `_ordered`, `_cron_days`, `_cron_times`, `_days_text`, `_unscheduled_flows`, `_failure_words`, `_watched_files`, `_hour`

### `legacy_audit.report.functional`

File: `legacy_audit/report/functional.py`

``legacy-audit report --type functional``: the functional document, for business readers.

A static, offline HTML site like the technical report (same theme, vendored Chart.js and Mermaid,
evidence links), written to ``runs/<id>/reports/functional/``. It reads two things:

- the **scan facts**, for every count, every screen and batch flow (screen -> services ->
  tables -> next screen; batch -> steps -> programs -> tables and files), the CRUD heat map, the
  batch calendar and the interface map;
- the **validated enrichment** (``functional``, ``classification``, ``flows``, ``overview``,
  ``assumptions``, ``narratives``), for the words: capabilities, actors, use cases, business
  rules, data entities, one plain-language story per screen and per batch, glossary.

A part whose enrichment stage is missing shows a placeholder naming the prompt to run, and the
scan-only parts still build, so the document can be built straight after a scan.

- `build_functional_report(run_dir: Path, inputs_dir: Path | None=None) -> Path`: Build the functional document for a run; returns its ``index.html``.

### `legacy_audit.report.pdf`

File: `legacy_audit/report/pdf.py`

``legacy-audit report --type pdf``: PDF copies of the HTML reports.

The HTML reports are printed by a browser in headless mode (Microsoft Edge, Chrome or Chromium),
so charts and diagrams look as they do on screen. Nothing is downloaded and the browser runs with
host names unresolvable, so the pages cannot reach the network. Without a browser the PDFs are a
coverage gap: skipped with a message, never an error.

Each HTML page is printed from a temporary copy (``_pdf-*.html`` next to it, removed afterwards)
that adds the paper size and ``window.LEGACY_AUDIT_PDF``, which tells the page scripts to print
up to ``pdf.max_table_rows`` rows per table. The multi-page reports (technical, functional) are
printed page by page and joined with ``pypdf`` behind a cover with contents, with bookmarks and
"page i of n" stamped on every page.

- **class `PdfError`**(Exception)
  A page could not be printed (browser failed, timed out or wrote nothing).
- **class `Browser`** `@dataclass`
  - fields: `path`, `label`, `windows_from_wsl`
- **class `PdfResult`** `@dataclass`
  - fields: `files`, `messages`, `browser`
- `is_wsl() -> bool`
- `candidates() -> list[str]`: Places a browser is looked for, best first, for this machine.
- `find_browser(configured: str | None=None) -> Browser | None`: ``pdf.browser_path`` when set (it must exist), else the first browser found.
- `missing_message(configured: str | None) -> str`
- **class `Printer`**
  - `__init__(browser: Browser, cfg: PdfConfig) -> None`
  - `command(url: str, pdf_arg: str, profile: str | None) -> list[str]`
  - `print_file(page: Path, pdf: Path) -> None`: Print an HTML file as it is (it must carry its own @page rules).
  - `print_page(page: Path, pdf: Path, *, deck: bool=False) -> None`: Print a report page through a temporary copy that adds the PDF settings.
- `page_css(cfg: PdfConfig) -> str`
- `inject(text: str, cfg: PdfConfig, *, deck: bool=False) -> str`: The page with the PDF settings added at the top of <head>.
- **class `Part`** `@dataclass`
  - fields: `title`, `page`, `level`, `pdf`, `pages`, `error`
- `page_title(page: Path) -> str`
- `parts_for(key: str, folder: Path, cfg: PdfConfig) -> list[Part]`: Pages of a multi-page report in menu order, detail pages after their main page.
- `join_report(printer: Printer, key: str, folder: Path, dest: Path, work: Path, run: dict[str, Any], app: str) -> list[str]`: Print every page of a multi-page report and join them into ``dest``; returns problems.
- `single_report(printer: Printer, key: str, page: Path, dest: Path, work: Path, app: str, run: dict[str, Any] | None=None) -> list[str]`: Summary report and management deck: one HTML page, one PDF.
- `build_pdfs(run_dir: Path, cfg: PdfConfig | None=None, reports: tuple[str, ...]=('summary', 'mgmt', 'functional', 'tech')) -> PdfResult`: Print the HTML reports of a run that exist into ``reports/pdf/``.
- internal helpers: `_label`, `_from_wsl`, `_mm_px`, `_cover_html`, `_entries`, `_cover`, `_link`, `_numbers_html`, `_sizes`, `_render_html`, `_page_count`, `_shrink`, `_sections`

### `legacy_audit.report.pptx`

File: `legacy_audit/report/pptx.py`

``legacy-audit report --type pptx``: the editable PowerPoint, built on a corporate template.

Python writes ``reports/mgmt/deck.json`` and builds ``reports/deck.pptx`` from it with
``python-pptx`` on the chosen template (``templates/*.potx``; see ``pptx_templates``). Every slide
uses one of the template's layouts, so the deck keeps the template's master, colours and fonts.

Mermaid source goes to the speaker notes. When no template is found the PPTX is skipped with a
message saying what to do; nothing else fails.

- `build_pptx(run_dir: Path, branding: Branding | None=None, config_dir: Path | None=None, template: str | None=None) -> PptxResult`: Build ``reports/deck.pptx`` for a run on a corporate template, or say why it was skipped.
- internal helpers: `_node`, `_mmdc`

### `legacy_audit.report.pptx_build`

File: `legacy_audit/report/pptx_build.py`

Build the management PPTX from deck.json on a corporate template (python-pptx).

The template's own sample slides are dropped and every slide is added from one of its layouts:
the cover, a contents slide (SUMMARY), a chapter divider per section (CHAPTER_1..4 in turn),
TEXT or TEXT_DOUBLE for content and END. Titles, footers and prose go into the layouts'
placeholders, so they take the template's fonts, sizes and colours. Charts are native PowerPoint
charts (bar, doughnut, line) so they stay editable; tables and heat maps are native tables; gauges
are doughnut charts; flows, capability maps, layers and the roadmap are native shapes; other
diagrams are PNG files rendered from Mermaid when mermaid-cli was available, else a note (the
Mermaid source is in the speaker notes). Every colour drawn is one of the template's theme colours
and every font is its heading font. Every number comes from deck.json, which comes from the scan.

- `theme(token: str | None) -> tuple[MSO_THEME_COLOR, float]`: A deck.json colour token as one of the template's theme colours (and a tint).
- `paint(cf: ColorFormat, token: str | None, tint: float | None=None) -> None`
- `kind_color(kind: str) -> MSO_THEME_COLOR`
- **class `Box`** `@dataclass`
  - fields: `x`, `y`, `w`, `h`
- `E(inches: float) -> Emu`
- `fmt(v: Any) -> str`
- `fit_size(texts: Iterable[str], w: float, h: float, base: int, floor: int=9) -> int`: The largest size (pt) at which the paragraphs roughly fit a w x h inch box.
- `style_run(run: Any, size: float | None=None, bold: bool | None=None, color: str | None=None, tint: float | None=None, white: bool=False) -> None`
- `write(tf: TextFrame, paras: list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]], *, wrap: bool=True, anchor: MSO_ANCHOR=MSO_ANCHOR.TOP, margin: float | None=None) -> None`: Fill a text frame: one paragraph per item, each with its run options.
- **class `Builder`**
  - `__init__(deck: dict[str, Any], template: Template, base_dir: Path) -> None`
  - `build(out: Path) -> int`
  - `cover(s: dict[str, Any] | None) -> None`
  - `contents() -> None`
  - `section(s: dict[str, Any], n: int) -> None`
  - `content(s: dict[str, Any]) -> None`
  - `block(slide: Slide, b: dict[str, Any], box: Box) -> None`
  - `draw_diagram(slide: Slide, b: dict[str, Any], box: Box) -> None`
- `fill_texty(tf: TextFrame, b: dict[str, Any], box: Box, textbox: bool=False) -> None`: Prose in the template's body styles: level 0 heading, 1 paragraph, 2 bullet.
- `heading(slide: Slide, text: str | None, box: Box) -> float`
- `note_box(slide: Slide, box: Box, paras: list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]]) -> None`
- `rect(slide: Slide, box: Box, fill: tuple[MSO_THEME_COLOR, float], line: tuple[MSO_THEME_COLOR, float] | None=None, shape: MSO_SHAPE=MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, radius: float | None=None) -> Any`
- `textbox(slide: Slide, box: Box, text: str, **opts: Any) -> Any`
- `draw_kpis(slide: Slide, b: dict[str, Any], box: Box) -> None`
- `draw_table(slide: Slide, b: dict[str, Any], box: Box) -> None`
- `draw_chart(slide: Slide, b: dict[str, Any], box: Box) -> None`
- `draw_gauges(slide: Slide, b: dict[str, Any], box: Box) -> None`: Share of a whole as a ring: a native doughnut chart with the percentage in the middle.
- `draw_capmap(slide: Slide, b: dict[str, Any], box: Box) -> None`: Domains as tinted groups; each capability a white tile with the domain's colour edge.
- `draw_heatmap(slide: Slide, b: dict[str, Any], box: Box) -> None`: A native table whose cell fill shows how much (seq) or how risky (risk); the text stays.
- `draw_flow(slide: Slide, b: dict[str, Any], box: Box) -> None`: A flow as columns of coloured boxes joined by arrows (all editable shapes).
- `draw_gantt(slide: Slide, b: dict[str, Any], box: Box) -> None`: Plan waves as bars on a month axis.

### `legacy_audit.report.pptx_templates`

File: `legacy_audit/report/pptx_templates.py`

Corporate PowerPoint templates the PPTX is built on.

Templates are ``.potx`` (or ``.pptx``) files. They are found, in order, in
``$LEGACY_AUDIT_TEMPLATES_DIR``, the copy packaged inside ``legacy_audit/_pptx_templates`` (wheel
installs) and ``templates/`` of a source checkout. ``branding.pptx_template`` in audit.yaml (or
``--template`` / the reports page) picks one by name (``blue``), file name or path; the default is
the first template found. Every slide is built on one of the template's own layouts, so the deck
carries its master, theme colours, fonts, pictures and logo and nothing else.

  The chosen template is missing or cannot be used.

  - fields: `id`, `label`, `path`

- `list_templates() -> list[Template]`: The templates found in the first folder that has any, sorted by name.
- `resolve_template(choice: str | None, config_dir: Path | None=None) -> Template`: The template for ``choice``: a label (``blue``), a file name or stem, or a path.
- `template_bytes(path: Path) -> io.BytesIO`: The template as a presentation package: a .potx differs only by its main content type.
- `thumbnail(path: Path) -> bytes | None`: The preview picture PowerPoint stores in the file (docProps/thumbnail.jpeg), if any.

### `legacy_audit.report.summary`

File: `legacy_audit/report/summary.py`

``legacy-audit report --type summary``: a five-part summary report, as HTML and PowerPoint.

1. **Project**: what the application is, its technology stack, and its modules (components)
   with a description, technology, complexity and lines of code;
2. **Database and queries**: SQL statements, PostgreSQL readiness, tables, databases;
3. **Integrations**: one row per interface with its purpose and description;
4. **Batches**: every batch once, with what it does and when it runs (``report/batches.py``);
5. **Dependency vulnerabilities**: the known vulnerabilities of the libraries, from OWASP
   Dependency-Check and OSV-Scanner merged into one list (``security/vulns.py``), each with the
   scanner(s) that found it; says plainly when neither scanner's results are there.

Each part has headline figures, charts and the data behind them (tables, and a CSV per table
next to the page). Every number comes from the scan (rule 1); descriptions come from the
Copilot enrichment when it exists, else from the scan, and say which.

The page is ``reports/summary/index.html``; its **PowerPoint** button downloads
``summary.pptx``, built at the same time on the corporate template chosen for the run
(``branding.pptx_template`` or ``--template``) with the same slide builder as the management
deck, so the PowerPoint follows the template's masters and layouts (decision 124).

- **class `Table`** `@dataclass`
  - fields: `key`, `title`, `columns`, `rows`, `note`, `empty`
- **class `Chart`** `@dataclass`
  - fields: `key`, `title`, `kind`, `labels`, `values`, `colors`, `unit`
- **class `Section`** `@dataclass`
  - fields: `key`, `title`, `audience`, `color`, `intro`, `kpis`, `charts`, `tables`, `source_note`, `alert`
- `to_deck(rd: RunData, sections: list[Section], branding: Branding) -> dict[str, Any]`: The summary as ``deck.json`` slides, for ``pptx_build.build_on_template``.
- **class `SummaryResult`** `@dataclass`
  - fields: `page`, `pptx`, `message`, `template`
- `build_sections(run_dir: Path) -> tuple[RunData, list[Section]]`
- `build_summary_report(run_dir: Path, branding: Branding | None=None, config_dir: Path | None=None, template: str | None=None) -> SummaryResult`: Write ``reports/summary/`` (index.html, summary.json, deck.json, CSVs, summary.pptx).
- internal class `_Summary` Methods: `__init__`, `description`, `_component_counts`, `_languages`, `module_description`, `project`, `_tables`, `data`, `integrations`, `_web_services`, `_idp`, `batch`, `_found_by`, `_library_modules`, `security`
- internal helpers: `_plan_text`, `_pct`, `_plural`, `_top`, `_eol`, `_cell`, `_env`, `_write_csv`

### `legacy_audit.report.tech`

File: `legacy_audit/report/tech.py`

``legacy-audit report --type tech``: a static, self-contained HTML site built from one run.

Pages are rendered with Jinja2 from ``tech_html/``; catalogues are written as ``data/*.js`` and
drawn by ``assets/report.js``; Chart.js and Mermaid are vendored in ``assets/vendor/``. The site
opens from disk (``file://``) with no server and no network. It is written to
``runs/<id>/reports/tech/``; when ``latest`` is a copy of that run (no symlinks on the machine),
the copy gets its own build so its relative links stay right.

- `build_tech_report(run_dir: Path, inputs_dir: Path | None=None) -> Path`: Build the site for a run; returns ``reports/tech/index.html`` of that run.
- `bar(chart_id: str, title: str, labels: list[str], values: list[float], colors: list[str] | str='series-1', *, label: str='Count', category: str='', unit: str='', horizontal: bool=False, note: str='') -> dict[str, Any]`: A one-series bar chart (``colors``: CSS token names, one per bar or one for all).
- internal class `_Pages` Methods: `__init__`, `_badges`, `_render`, `_link`, `_tile`, `overview`, `_band_chart`, `_gauges`, `components`, `_radars`, `architecture`, `flow_ctx`, `flows`, `data_model`, `summary_top_tables`, `catalogue`, `postgresql`, `security`, `analysis`, `findings`, `appendix`

### `legacy_audit.report.visuals`

File: `legacy_audit/report/visuals.py`

Graphics shared by the technical report and the functional document.

Chart specs are drawn by ``assets/report.js`` with the vendored Chart.js; gauges, heat maps,
the risk matrix, the batch week calendar and Gantt bars are plain HTML and CSS (no script), so
they print and work without JavaScript. Every value shown comes from the facts or the validated
enrichment passed in; nothing here counts anything new.

Colours are CSS tokens (``series-1`` ... ``series-8`` for identity, ``seq-*`` for magnitude,
``good`` / ``warning`` / ``serious`` / ``critical`` for status), so light and dark themes both
work; the PPTX uses the light values of the same tokens (``deck_builder.PALETTE``).

- `icon(name: str) -> Markup`
- `chart(chart_id: str, title: str, kind: str, labels: list[str], values: list[Any] | None=None, *, colors: list[str] | str='series-1', datasets: list[dict[str, Any]] | None=None, label: str='Count', category: str='', unit: str='', horizontal: bool=False, note: str='', tall: bool=False, **extra: Any) -> dict[str, Any]`: A chart for the ``chart`` macro: ``kind`` is bar, stacked, doughnut, radar or bubble. ``values`` (one series) or ``datasets`` ([{label, values, color}]) also fill the "Show as table" view, so no chart is colour-only.
- `gauge(label: str, part: float, whole: float, color: str='good', sub: str='') -> dict[str, Any]`: A ring showing ``part`` of ``whole`` as a percentage (both from the facts).
- `heat_level(n: int, top: int) -> int`: 1..6 shade for a positive count relative to the largest one (0 = empty).
- `risk_matrix(risks: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> dict[str, Any]`: Severity (rows) x likelihood (columns) with the risk ids in each cell.
- `gantt(waves: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> dict[str, Any]`: Plan waves as bars on a month axis (start and duration from the plan).

### `legacy_audit.rules.engine`

File: `legacy_audit/rules/engine.py`

Turns rule packs into findings: fact rules over collections, text rules from cached hits.

Every run re-evaluates the rules (they are cheap), so switching a rule off or changing its
severity in ``audit.yaml`` takes effect without re-analysing files. The same switches apply to
findings that analyzers and the linker raise themselves (``config-credential``,
``unresolved-reference``, ``analyzer-error``).

- `matches(item: Mapping[str, Any], where: Mapping[str, Any]) -> bool`
- `render(template: str, item: Mapping[str, Any]) -> str`
- `finding(rule: Rule, item: Mapping[str, Any], key: str) -> Finding`
- `evaluate(rules: Iterable[Rule], collection: Callable[[str], list[dict[str, Any]]], hits: Iterable[tuple[str, str, int, str]]) -> list[Finding]`: Findings for fact rules (``collection(name)`` gives the items) and for text hits ``(file, rule id, line, text)``.
- `apply_config(findings: Iterable[Finding], cfg: AuditConfig) -> list[Finding]`: Drop disabled rules, apply severity changes, de-duplicate by id, sort.
- internal class `_Fields`: ``{field}`` and ``{a.b}`` over a dict; unknown fields render as ``?``. Methods: `get_field`
- internal helpers: `_get`, `_number`, `_check`, `_location`

### `legacy_audit.rules.packs`

File: `legacy_audit/rules/packs.py`

Rule packs: YAML files in ``rules/`` (shipped with the tool) plus an optional team folder
(``rules.packs_dir``) whose rules replace ours by id or add new ones.

A rule matches either

- facts: ``match: {entity: <collection>, where: {<field>: <condition>}}``, evaluated every run
  over the linked facts (and the metric collections ``units``, ``dead_code``, ``binaries``); or
- text: ``pattern: {regex: ..., languages: [...]}``, evaluated per file by the ``patterns``
  analyzer and cached with the file (the patterns' hash is part of the cache key).

Conditions: a plain value means equal; otherwise a mapping of ``eq``, ``ne``, ``in``,
``not_in``, ``regex``, ``gt``, ``gte``, ``lt``, ``lte``, ``exists``, ``empty``, ``contains``.

- **class `FactMatch`**(_Strict)
  - fields: `entity`, `where`
- **class `TextPattern`**(_Strict)
  - fields: `regex`, `ignore_case`, `multiline`, `languages`, `ignore`, `unless_file`, `max_per_file`
  - `compiled() -> re.Pattern[str]`
- **class `Rule`**(_Strict)
  - fields: `id`, `severity`, `category`, `message`, `remediation`, `severity_field`, `match`, `pattern`
- **class `Pack`**(_Strict)
  - fields: `pack`, `description`, `rules`, `data`
- `builtin_dir() -> Path`: ``legacy_audit/_rules`` in an installed wheel, the repository's ``rules/`` otherwise.
- `load_pack(name: str, team_dir: Path | None=None) -> Pack`
- `text_rules(enabled: list[str], team_dir: Path | None) -> list[Rule]`: Every text rule of the enabled packs (disabled ones too: switching a rule off is applied when findings are built, so it needs no re-scan).
- `rules_key(rules: list[Rule]) -> str`: Hash of the text patterns: part of the file-cache key, so changing one re-scans.
- internal class `_Strict`
- internal helpers: `_read`, `_load`

### `legacy_audit.rules.pg`

File: `legacy_audit/rules/pg.py`

PostgreSQL grading of SQL statements and stored objects (rules in ``pg-rules.yaml``).

- **class `Construct`** `@dataclass(frozen=True)`
  - fields: `id`, `pattern`, `grade`, `reason`, `valid_in_pg`
- `constructs(data: dict[str, Any]) -> list[Construct]`
- `grade(st: SqlStatement, rules: list[Construct]) -> Graded`: (grade, reason, suggested PostgreSQL text).
- **class `GradeCache`**
  Grades of earlier runs, by statement and rule set: a re-run grades only new SQL.
  - `__init__(path: Path, rules_key: str) -> None`
  - `hash(key: tuple[Any, ...]) -> str`
  - `get(h: str) -> Graded | None`
  - `put(h: str, result: Graded) -> None`
  - `close() -> None`
- `rules_key(data: dict[str, Any]) -> str`
- `grade_all(statements: list[SqlStatement], objects: list[DbObject], data: dict[str, Any], *, workers: int=1, cache_file: Path | None=None, cancel: threading.Event | None=None) -> None`: Grade in place. Identical statements are graded once, statements graded by an earlier run come from ``cache_file``, and the rest are graded across ``workers`` processes.
- internal helpers: `_transpile`, `_worst`, `_grade_text`, `_key`, `_setup`, `_grade_one`

### `legacy_audit.security.versions`

File: `legacy_audit/security/versions.py`

Version comparison close to Maven's ordering, and simple range expressions.

``1.2.17 < 1.2.18``, ``2.0-beta1 < 2.0-rc1 < 2.0 = 2.0.0 = 2.0.Final < 2.0-sp1 < 2.0.1``.
Ranges are comma-separated bounds that must all hold: ``"<2"``, ``">=3.0,<3.5"``,
``"<=5.3.39"``; ``"*"`` matches any version (also an unknown one).

- `compare(a: str, b: str) -> int`
- `sort_versions(versions: list[str]) -> list[str]`
- `in_range(version: str | None, spec: str | None) -> bool | None`: True/False, or None when the version is unknown and the range is not ``*``.
- internal helpers: `_parts`, `_rank`

### `legacy_audit.security.vulns`

File: `legacy_audit/security/vulns.py`

Known vulnerabilities per library from OWASP Dependency-Check and OSV-Scanner.

Reports are imported from ``audit-inputs/security/*.json`` (the kind is detected from the
content) or produced by running the tools when they are installed. Both work offline: the
Dependency-Check run uses ``--noupdate`` and OSV-Scanner (2.x) ``--offline`` unless the config says
otherwise. A tool that is not installed, fails or has no database is a coverage gap
(:class:`VulnerabilitySource` with status ``missing``/``failed``), never a crash and never a
silent "no vulnerabilities".

- **class `ReportEntry`** `@dataclass`
  Vulnerabilities reported for one dependency, with the keys used to match a library.
  - fields: `sha1`, `purls`, `file_name`, `vulnerabilities`
- **class `Report`** `@dataclass`
  - fields: `tool`, `path`, `database_date`, `entries`
- `detect_kind(data: Any) -> str | None`
- `parse_dependency_check(data: dict[str, Any], path: str) -> Report`
- `parse_osv(data: dict[str, Any], path: str) -> Report`
- `load_report(path: Path, display: str) -> Report | None`
- `find_tool(configured: str | None, names: tuple[str, ...]) -> str | None`
- `missing_detail(configured: str | None, names: tuple[str, ...]) -> str`: Why a tool was not found: "not installed", or the configured path that does not exist (and where one is on PATH, so the fix is plain).
- `run_dependency_check(cfg: DependencyCheckConfig, scan_dirs: list[Path], out_dir: Path, project: str) -> tuple[Report | None, VulnerabilitySource]`
- `run_osv_scanner(cfg: OsvScannerConfig, scan_dirs: list[Path], out_dir: Path) -> tuple[Report | None, VulnerabilitySource]`
- `failure_hint(tool: str, output: str) -> str | None`
- `purl(lib: Library) -> str | None`
- `apply_reports(libraries: list[Library], reports: list[Report]) -> int`: Attach vulnerabilities to libraries (by SHA-1, then package URL, then jar file name); merge duplicates by CVE id. Returns how many report entries matched no library.
- internal helpers: `_severity_from_score`, `_norm_severity`, `_osv_fixed`, `_run`, `_file_name`, `_purl_key`, `_merge`

### `legacy_audit.store.lock`

File: `legacy_audit/store/lock.py`

One scan at a time per output folder.

The lock is an OS file lock on ``runs/.lock`` (``fcntl`` on Linux/macOS, ``msvcrt`` on Windows),
so it is released when the process ends, even after a crash or a killed terminal; a stale lock
file never blocks the next scan.

- **class `ScanBusy`**(Exception)
- **class `ScanLock`**
  - `__init__(runs_dir: Path) -> None`
  - `acquire() -> ScanLock`
  - `release() -> None`

Run folders: ``<output>/runs/<run-id>/`` plus a ``latest`` pointer.

``latest`` is a symlink to the newest run where the OS allows it, otherwise a copy of the run
folder (Windows without developer mode). ``runs/LATEST`` always holds the newest run id, and is
what the tool itself reads.
